fragments.text: **CHAT-001 — Teams, Discord, Telegram and workplace chat.** Microsoft Teams is supported through Microsoft's current mechanisms, because Microsoft is retiring Office 365 connectors (incoming webhooks). The first is a Teams Workflows webhook URL (the "post to a channel when a webhook request is received" workflow), to which Uptime posts Adaptive Cards. The second is the Uptime Teams app, which posts to a chosen channel or chat through the Bot Framework after a Teams admin installs it. A legacy Office 365 connector URL is accepted only with a "retiring connector" label. The label is shown on the destination, in the MIGRATE-001 preview and in drill results, with steps to create a Workflows URL. A connector URL that starts refusing posts is shown as failed with Microsoft's response, never as delivered. Discord, Telegram (Bot API with the buyer's bot token and chat or group ID), Google Chat and Mattermost destinations carry monitor, location, failed assertion, severity, incident key and authenticated evidence link with tested trigger/recovery/drill formatting. Per-channel scopes, credential rotation, rate limits and delivery uncertainty follow the same custody rules as Slack. **Acceptance evidence:** Configure each named connector, including a Telegram bot posting to a group chat, a Teams Workflows URL and the Uptime Teams app in a channel, through the owner console, drill it, fail and recover a monitor, return a provider error and rotate credentials; inspect channel readback, correlation and distinct acknowledgment/receipt states. Import an UptimeRobot Teams contact with a legacy connector URL and see the retiring-connector label and replacement steps; make that URL refuse posts and see a failed outcome with the response.

**PHONE-001 — US SMS and voice alerts.** SMS and voice calls sent from PHONE-002's Uptime-provided registered US sender (or, optionally, a buyer-connected Twilio account) to verified US E.164 numbers deliver incident context and secure acknowledgment with consent, quiet hours, opt-out, per-team USD budgets and visible provider/carrier outcomes. Repeats and call escalation follow the buyer policy and Oncall handoff; Uptime does not act as a carrier or guarantee receipt. Usage is metered and budgeted under COST-001. This clause inherits the SMS fallback acceptance from DELIVERY-002. **Acceptance evidence:** In a new workspace with no provider account, verify a real US mobile number and trigger SMS/voice and acknowledgment on that handset (PHONE-002). At the provider edge, simulate opt-out, spend cap, a failed carrier and an uncertain call result; inspect no unauthorized sends/charges and visible unresolved follow-up.

**PHONE-002 — Uptime-provided compliant US sender.** SMS and voice alerts work on day one in a new workspace, with no buyer provider account and no buyer carrier registration. Uptime runs a managed telephony relay, operated with Twilio in the same way as the RER mail relay used for email. Its alert SMS go out from a US A2P 10DLC-registered brand and campaign or a verified toll-free number, and its calls use a voice caller ID with STIR/SHAKEN attestation. The console shows the sender number, its registration state and a contact card recipients can save. Each recipient number is verified by a one-time code before it receives any alert. Uptime records consent, verification time and the opt-in text shown. STOP, HELP and START are honored at the carrier and in Uptime: an opted-out number is shown as opted out and receives nothing until it opts back in. Every attempt records the carrier delivery receipt (delivered, undelivered with the carrier error code, or unknown) and the call result (answered, busy, no answer or failed). Uptime owns and monitors registration status, sender changes and provider throughput. A suspension or filtering spike is shown to every affected owner, and the incident goes to the route's other channels and its DELIVERY-002 fallback chain. Connecting the buyer's own Twilio account and registered messaging service remains optional. Those credentials stay under installation-local custody, outcome reporting is the same, and Uptime never sends from a buyer account the buyer has not connected. This clause inherits the SMS fallback acceptance from DELIVERY-002. **Acceptance evidence:** In a new workspace with no provider account, verify a real US mobile number on each of AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile by one-time code. Confirm an outage: each handset receives the SMS and the voice call, with carrier delivery receipt and answered-call result recorded. Reply STOP and see further SMS stop and the opt-out shown; HELP returns the sender identification; START resumes. The console shows the registered sender and its state. Each send is metered at COST-001's shown USD price. Connect a buyer-owned Twilio account and see the alert sent from the buyer's number with the same outcomes.

**MOBILE-001 — Mobile operator access and push.** Responsive operator flows and native iOS/Android clients support secure sign-in honoring ACCESS-003 second factors, monitor/incident evidence, pause/maintenance controls and push alerts via APNs/FCM; Pushover and Pushbullet are selectable provider destinations. Expired tokens, offline reads, revoked sessions and notification permissions have honest states;
privileged actions retain server-side authorization and audit.

**Acceptance evidence:** Install the iOS and Android apps from their public App Store and Google Play listings; on those devices and 390-pixel web, receive a test push and open its exact incident, acknowledge via the configured responder handoff, go offline, revoke a session and deny push permission; inspect stale data labels and failed delivery. Drill Pushover and Pushbullet separately.

**ONCALL-001 — Responder handoff and automatic resolution.** Native [Oncall](https://github.com/just-every/run-oncall), PagerDuty Events API v2 and Splunk On-Call connectors hand confirmed failures to the buyer-selected service with stable deduplication key, severity, service/team mapping, regional/step evidence and authenticated attachments. Handoff acknowledgment and responder status remain separate. Recovery resolves the same remote incident; elapsed-time/team-availability/origin escalation invokes the configured responder policy rather than implementing rotations here. This clause inherits the PagerDuty destination-kind acceptance from DELIVERY-002. **Acceptance evidence:** Cause a confirmed failure and repeats through each named connector, interrupt the response, receive acknowledgment and recover; inspect one remote incident with evidence, correct policy and resolution, visible failed/uncertain handoffs and no imported-event replay.

**ct scope ruling, 25 October 2026:** ONCALL-001 receives connector-native handoff-check and configured responder-escalation policy, including handoff attempts/outcomes and the existing PagerDuty destination-kind inheritance. Its scheduling and outcomes must feed FOLLOWUP-001’s incident timeline and next-due projection and READAPI-001’s incident reads. Handoff acknowledgment remains separate from responder status, and recovery resolves the same remote incident.

**LAMP-001 — Status communication through Lamp.** Map monitors/services to [Lamp](https://github.com/just-every/run-lamp) or Atlassian Statuspage components and send signed idempotent confirmed incident/maintenance/recovery updates with evidence, source timestamps and confidence. The buyer chooses automatic publication or approval in Lamp; branded pages, subscriptions, subscriber updates and public narrative remain there. A stale probe never publishes a false recovery. An INCIDENT-001 comment reaches Lamp or Statuspage only through its explicit per-comment "Publish to status page" action. It is sent as an incident update with the member's chosen status and an idempotency key per comment version, on the same approval path, and its outcome is shown on the comment. **Acceptance evidence:** Map components, trigger a confirmed outage, replay an event, interrupt delivery and recover; inspect one Lamp/Statuspage incident, the selected approval/publication path and subscriber update there, with failed handoffs visible in Uptime. Publish an INCIDENT-001 comment and see one incident update in Lamp and in Statuspage, with the publication outcome on the comment. Replay the publish and see no duplicate; leave another comment unpublished and see nothing sent.

**AUTOMATION-001 — Zapier, Make and custom automation.** Versioned signed webhook events, WEBHOOK-001 custom-template webhook requests and supported Zapier/Make triggers/actions expose confirmed failure, recovery, expiring asset and due follow-up, with least-scope tokens, event IDs, replay controls and bounded outcomes. Owners can test, pause and revoke automations; downstream work cannot rewrite evidence or silently create duplicate customer messages. **Acceptance evidence:** Connect a Zapier and Make workflow through the supported connector, run failure/recovery and an expiry warning, replay callbacks and revoke access; inspect one downstream action per event and durable failed/stopped execution.

**WEBHOOK-001 — Custom webhook requests and payload templates.** A webhook destination sets its HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT or PATCH), its delivery mode (JSON body, form-encoded fields or query-string parameters) and up to 10 custom headers (4 KiB in total). Header values such as `Authorization` or `X-Api-Key` are installation-local secrets: they are encrypted at rest under NOTIFY-001's credential custody, masked after save and never logged, exported or placed in evidence. Its body or parameter template draws on a documented, versioned variable set. The variables cover monitor ID, name, URL, type and tags; alert type (down, up, test, expiry warning, slow) with UptimeRobot-compatible numeric codes and friendly names; alert details (the plain-language down reason); alert start time in UTC and the owner's US time zone; alert duration in seconds and human-readable form; incident key, stable event ID and console link; failed locations and each location's outcome; HTTP status code; response time; failed assertion; SSL certificate expiry date and days left; domain expiry date and days left; and heartbeat last-receipt time. UptimeRobot's notification variables (`*monitorID*`, `*monitorURL*`, `*monitorFriendlyName*`, `*alertType*`, `*alertTypeFriendlyName*`, `*alertDetails*`, `*alertDuration*`, `*alertDateTime*`, `*httpStatusCode*`, `*sslExpiryDate*`, `*sslExpiryDaysLeft*` and the rest of its published list) are accepted as aliases. A variable with no Uptime equivalent is named at save and in the MIGRATE-001 preview; it is never silently rendered empty. Every substituted value is escaped for where it lands. In JSON bodies that means JSON string escaping, with quotes, backslashes and control characters escaped and `<`, `>` and `&` written as Unicode escapes. Form and query values are percent-encoded. A header value containing CR or LF is refused. A JSON template that does not parse after substitution with sample values is refused at save. The console preview renders the exact request (method, URL, headers with secret values masked, and body) for sample trigger, recovery, expiry and slow events. A test send delivers it to the receiver and shows the status code and a bounded response excerpt without changing monitor state. Optional HMAC-SHA256 signing (timestamp and signature headers over the exact rendered bytes) applies on top of any template; NOTIFY-001's default signed JSON envelope remains one template choice. Requests follow NETWORK-001 destination rules, DELIVERY-001/DELIVERY-002 attempt semantics (the stable event ID is a variable and can be sent as an idempotency header) and ROUTING-001/ROUTING-002 route selection. Templates, method, mode and header names travel in archives; header values and signing keys do not. **Acceptance evidence:** Import an UptimeRobot webhook contact whose custom JSON POST value uses `*monitorFriendlyName*`, `*alertType*` and `*alertDetails*` and which sends an `X-Api-Key` header. Fail and recover a monitor: the controlled receiver gets the same field names, header and content type it got from UptimeRobot, with values substituted. A monitor named with quotes and `<script>` arrives correctly escaped, and the body parses as JSON. Query-string and form modes arrive as parameters, and GET mode sends no body. A header value containing CR/LF is refused at save. An unmappable variable is named in the migration preview and at save. The preview matches the received request byte for byte apart from masked secrets. The signed variant verifies with its HMAC. An archive export contains the template and header names but no header value.

fragments.text: **MANAGE-001 — Monitor and contact API.** Authenticated public product APIs create/read/update/pause monitors and manage alert destinations with the same validation, revisions, secret custody and authorization as the console. Bad input returns actionable errors without partial writes. Reading uptime, response-time and incident data, and the versioned, key-authenticated read API, are READAPI-001's. **Acceptance evidence:** Use the owner API to create/edit/pause a monitor and rotate a contact, read back its revision and attempt signed-out/cross-origin mutations; inspect atomic refusal and no exposed endpoint secrets.

**READAPI-001 — Versioned read API for uptime, response times and incidents.** A documented, versioned REST API at `/api/v1` gives dashboards, customer portals, SLA scripts and third-party integrations the same monitoring figures as the console.
It is described by an OpenAPI 3.1 document served at `/api/v1/openapi.json` and in the public `/docs`.
Requests authenticate with bearer API keys created under ACCESS-001.
A key belongs to one workspace and carries explicit scopes; `monitoring:read` is read-only.
A key can be limited further to tags or monitors and given an expiry.
It is shown once, stored hashed, revocable immediately, and its last use is recorded.
Creating one requires ACCESS-003 step-up.
The API offers these reads.
Monitors: `GET /api/v1/monitors` and `GET /api/v1/monitors/{id}`, with current state, last check and coverage.
Uptime: per-monitor `GET /api/v1/monitors/{id}/uptime` and bulk `GET /api/v1/uptime` for up to 500 monitors.

Each takes a named period (24 hours, 7, 30 or 90 days, month, quarter or year to date, last month) or a custom `from`/`to`, and an IANA time zone that defaults to the owner's US zone and handles daylight saving.
Each returns availability, observed, down, Unknown, paused and maintenance seconds, slow time (SLOW-001), incident count and the REPORT-001 denominator policy.
An optional `source` parameter selects the HISTORY-001 source segment, Uptime's own segment and the labeled blended figure, never the blended figure alone.
The accepted `source` query-value set in the retained API is empty: no value is accepted on per-monitor uptime/report, bulk uptime, response-time or incident reads.
`Uptime` and `restored Uptime history` are response labels, not accepted query values; the definition-import API's `source` vocabulary does not apply here.

The request schema refuses any supplied `source`, including unknown `not-a-source` and currently unavailable `UptimeRobot`, with HTTP 400 and the named reason `Unexpected query parameter`, followed by that route's allowed parameters.
Source selection remains required before this clause is done:
the OpenAPI document and public guide must list every accepted value exactly, including each supported HISTORY-001 source and the Uptime/blended selection.

An unknown or currently unavailable value must be refused with a reason naming the unknown value or unavailable source, never silently ignored, replaced by Uptime-only data or returned as an empty successful result.
Response times: `GET /api/v1/monitors/{id}/response-times`, by location or across locations.
It returns min, mean, p50, p95, p99 and max per bucket at raw, 1-minute, 5-minute, 1-hour or 1-day resolution, over ranges up to 90 days.
A request beyond 10,000 points per response is refused with a 400 naming the bound, and is never truncated.
Incidents: `GET /api/v1/incidents` and `GET /api/v1/incidents/{id}`.

They return start, end, duration in seconds, EVIDENCE-002's plain-language cause, failed locations, owner, acknowledgment, INCIDENT-001 root cause and comments, the FOLLOWUP-001 timeline and source (Uptime or imported).
The list is filterable by monitor, tag, date range, state and root-cause category.
Lists use cursor pagination with stable ordering and a documented maximum page size.
Uptime and incident reads can also return CSV (`Accept: text/csv`).
Every figure is computed by the same code as the console and REPORT-001, so the API, the console and a downloaded report agree exactly for the same monitor, period, time zone and source.
Rate limits are documented per key and reported in `RateLimit` headers.
Exceeding one returns 429 with `Retry-After`, and the request has no effect.
A `monitoring:read` key refuses every mutating method with 403 and writes nothing.
A key for one workspace gets 404 for another workspace's monitors and incidents, and a tag- or monitor-limited key sees only its selection.
A breaking change ships only as a new version.
The old version keeps working for at least 12 months and carries `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers in the meantime.
The docs map each UptimeRobot v2 `getMonitors` read (uptime ratios, response times, logs) and v3 stats and incident read to its equivalent, so a migrating buyer can repoint a dashboard or script.
METRICS-001's Prometheus and Grafana integration reads the same figures.
**Acceptance evidence:** Cause known outages, an Unknown gap, a maintenance window and slow responses on a monitor.
With a `monitoring:read` key, call the API for 24-hour, 7-day, 30-day and custom-period uptime in America/Chicago, the bulk uptime read, the response-time series by location at two resolutions,
and the incident list filtered by root cause, then page through it.
Compare each result with the REPORT-001 console figure, the downloaded CSV and the immutable slots: they match exactly.
Ask for the HISTORY-001 segment on a migrated monitor and see source, Uptime and labeled blended figures.

Make one request per exact accepted `source` value in the OpenAPI schema, plus an unknown value and a currently unavailable source; accepted values select the documented figures, while each refused request names its reason and returns no substituted or empty success.

Until source selection ships, the accepted-value set is empty: requests with `source=not-a-source` and `source=UptimeRobot` both return HTTP 400 with `Unexpected query parameter`; this refusal proves no HISTORY-001 segment support.
A POST, PATCH or DELETE with the read-only key returns 403 and nothing changes.
Exceeding the documented limit returns 429 with Retry-After.
A key for one workspace cannot read another workspace's monitors, a tag-limited key sees only its tag, and a revoked key is refused at once.
An over-bound response-time request is refused, not truncated.
Repoint a script that read UptimeRobot `getMonitors` uptime ratios to the documented equivalent and get the same periods.

**ct scope ruling, 25 October 2026:** Incident reads retain FOLLOWUP-001’s authoritative next-due kind/time and timeline. Current DELIVERY-002 fallback escalation and ROUTING-002 notification/reminder behavior remain acceptance obligations; ONCALL-001 handoff scheduling remains an open dependency, not an exemption.

HTTP Digest credentials map to API-002, and "ignore SSL errors" maps to NETWORK-002's labeled exception. The read-back also names each UptimeRobot API read the account's keys used and its READAPI-001 equivalent, so dashboards and scripts can be repointed before cutover. A read-back report lists every monitor, contact, notify-only seat, member, status page, subscriber count, maintenance window and integration as migrated, handed off or unsupported with its reason. **Acceptance evidence:** Use an authorized UptimeRobot export/API account, preview paginated extraction, reconcile counts and every unsupported field, apply paused definitions, authorize secrets, compare both products and cut over without duplicate alerts; retain rollback. An account with two status pages (one password-protected, with subscribers) and Telegram and SMS contacts previews both pages and every contact; after approval Lamp holds both pages with mapped components, the custom domain switches with valid TLS, the read-back accounts for every record and no subscriber receives a duplicate or import notice. A webhook contact with a custom JSON POST value and an `X-Api-Key` header passes WEBHOOK-001's receiver journey. An HTTP monitor with SSL and domain reminders gains matching TLS-001 and DOMAIN-001 monitors. A 60-day log CSV passes HISTORY-001's report journey. An incident with a comment and root cause imports as labeled source history, or the preview names the unexposed field. An account with two login seats and three notify-only seats reads back two pending invitations with mapped roles and three notify-only destinations, with no member reported dropped. A legacy Teams connector URL is flagged with replacement steps.

`seed.json → externals` declares the source-level outbound data categories. Public HTTP(S) monitors and status-only canaries resolve each public target, validate every redirect hop, and send the configured method, path/query, allowed headers and request body to the target. A request credential is sent only to its exact owner-authorized monitor origin; cross-origin redirects strip it, custom headers and body. Ordinary checks read bounded response status, headers and body for assertions without retaining raw bodies in observations; EVIDENCE-002 stores a separately retained, redacted failure excerpt with bounded request/response and timing facts. Its opt-in isolated browser renders that received excerpt as an encrypted PNG without another target request; scripts, styling, media and network are blocked. Snapshot access, retention, archive portability and erasure follow EVIDENCE-002. A canary is a status-only `GET` with no credential, custom headers or body and reads zero response-body bytes. DNS queries reveal only the hostnames being resolved plus source network address and lookup timing to the resolver configured for the runner.

TCP and TLS monitors connect to the owner's public host and port at its validated address: TCP sends nothing and may read up to 512 bytes of banner (256 printable characters kept); TLS sends a ClientHello naming the host and keeps certificate subject, issuer, names, validity and fingerprint. DNS monitors send the monitored name and type to the selected public resolvers (Cloudflare, Google) over HTTPS and, when chosen, one non-recursive query over TCP to the zone's authoritative server; bounded normalized records are kept. Domain monitors send the domain name to IANA's RDAP bootstrap, its registry and the registrar record the registry links, over HTTPS; the expiry date, source and update time, status values and redaction or conflict are kept. These flows are declared in `seed.json` as `public-protocol-targets`, `dns-over-https-resolvers` and `rdap-registries`.

Discovery is read-only and runs on the owner's runner; a hosted demo, which has no runner, runs the same crawl and limits in the Worker over public GET/HEAD requests without credentials. It may follow any validated public redirect from the initial URL; subsequent crawls are bounded to the final/input registrable domains and linked status hosts, subject to robots and request/time/body limits. It may request robots files, permitted pages, JSON/spec documents, conventional API hosts and status hosts. Bounded response content is parsed in runner memory. Only validated definitions, hostnames, URLs, short notes and request/timing summaries return to the Worker; raw HTML, response headers and page bodies do not. The Worker stores only the bounded derived result. No supplied HTML is rendered as console HTML.

An owner-authorized discovery source (DISCOVERY-001) is read only when the owner runs it, and only by the owner's runner. A domain source sends DNS queries for the domain's usual host names to the runner's resolver, then GET or HEAD requests to the hosts that resolve to public addresses. A robots/sitemap or OpenAPI source reads those public files and requests the routes they list. All of these requests follow the discovery fetcher's robots, budget and public-address rules. A provider source sends the provider only its account identifiers (a zone ID, repository, project, site, or application and deployment group) and documented read-only list requests. CodeDeploy: ListDeployments and BatchGetDeployments, signed with Signature Version 4.

A slot outcome and scheduled confirmation/recovery streaks are pure projections of stored attempts, recalculated on each arrival in chronological slot order. Revisions are immutable, so changing the setting applies to monitors saved afterwards and never rewrites a saved one. The setting is installation-local and does not travel in archives; the URL a revision carries does. Existing public throttling still returns 429.

`seed.json → deploy.publicPaths` declares sessionless documents, authentication routes, assets, health, credentialed runner and heartbeat APIs, owner-editor configuration, redirects and local-only development endpoints. The server still performs each route's normal authentication check after the rate-limit admission. `seed.json → limits.publicRequestsPerMinutePerIp` sets an owner-tunable maximum for each path class in a 60-second D1 window. Hosted requests use a keyed hash of the Cloudflare client-IP header; missing or malformed values share an unknown-client bucket. Local requests share a loopback bucket regardless of forwarded headers. Excess requests receive 429 and `Retry-After`; unavailable counter storage returns 503. Only expired public-rate counters are removed automatically; those counters are short-lived operational state and not product records. Limits are marked estimated and not load-tested, and do not establish capacity.

Each Node runner signs purpose-separated enrollment and results with its own scoped key. Identity, declared network label, revocation and credentials stay installation-local. Legacy key-only clients resolve to the migrated first runner; they have no authority over other runners' probes. See C4 above.

Slot identity is monitor/revision/due time; attempt identity includes slot/probe/attempt. Manual requests have distinct identities. The acceptance window is bounded; expired, foreign or contradictory attempts are rejected and the first accepted copy wins. Edited or paused inflight work remains historical evidence and cannot change current state or events. Missed cadence is counted without fabricated catchup results. A scheduled check is due no sooner than one interval after the monitor's previous scheduled check was claimed and after its first attempt reported starting; after an edit, the shorter of the old and new intervals applies, so a late check moves later due times back rather than running checks closer together; equal runner and Worker clocks make the reported-start floor exact. Backward clock movement waits for due time; future evidence cannot establish health.

Observation, state and outbox writes share one durable transaction. Migration history is permanent. Completion verifies the immutable definition, fixed probe denominator, exact assertion bundle, outcome, clock bounds and transport limits. Live latency validation uses the larger retained elapsed measure. Historical archive compatibility does not relax live validation.

Every private document, mutation, observation read and export requires server-side operator or scoped runner authority. Missing configuration fails closed. Browser mutations bind the configured origin and reject cross-site requests. Loopback is not authentication. Shared Base operator-auth owns operator credentials and sessions; product policy must not silently grant additional roles. Signed reporting identifies the holder of the runner key; it does not prove an uncompromised runner.

Private-runner public HTTP(S) checks validate every A/AAAA answer and redirect hop, reject unsafe or mixed address sets, pin numeric sockets and retain original Host and SNI. Certificate verification is the default; NETWORK-002’s owner-saved fingerprint, private CA or acknowledged ignore exception applies only to the initial HTTPS origin, records bounded certificate/error facts and never authorizes credentials. Cross-origin redirects restore default verification. These exceptions require a private runner; the hosted Worker refuses them. Proxy environments are bypassed. HTTPS downgrade is rejected; an origin change strips credentials, custom headers, request body and mutating method. DNS, redirects, body and retries have bounded execution. Responses are limited to 64 KiB; compressed responses are rejected. An external check asserts status 200 only, so it stops at the response headers and neither reads nor keeps the body, however large the page; every other guarantee here applies to it unchanged. Independent network isolation remains an operating requirement. Hosted HTTP(S) and keyword monitors without runner-local credentials default to the Cloudflare Worker. Owner-console requests prompt due work; its one-minute Cron schedule continues background work, but initial Cloudflare activation can take up to about two hours. The Worker validates all public DNS answers and every redirect and uses Cloudflare’s public Internet fetch transport with certificate verification, no private-network binding, no cached probe response and the same time, body and assertion bounds. Numeric socket pinning is the private runner’s transport guarantee. The Worker is one network vantage; it uses the same configured canary and scheduled evidence rules and cannot supply independent regional agreement. TCP, DNS, TLS and domain checks also run in the Worker or an assigned private runner. Worker TCP cannot reach Cloudflare addresses, Worker TLS cannot inspect a TLS 1.3-only service, and a registry without RDAP has no WHOIS fallback; these cases remain Unknown as the protocol Status rows describe. Browser flows and checks using runner-local credentials require an assigned private runner.
Synthetic checks retain a separate live process/custody grant, exact path/port identity, expiry, GET/HEAD-only and no-redirect boundary. Grant authority is rechecked on every attempt.

Request headers/body, Basic, Digest and bearer authentication, OAuth 2.0 client-credentials or refresh-token acquisition, JWT signing and mTLS client certificates/keys use protected runner-local regular files with exact monitor-ID and origin binding, expiry and rotation checks. OAuth token requests use their configured HTTPS token endpoint; refresh state stays local. Credential failures remain distinct runner errors, and neither token material nor client private keys enter evidence or exports. Credential authority comes from the authenticated task envelope while its assigned probe and acceptance window are valid; another monitor on the same runner cannot use the same reference to obtain the credential. Setup runs numbered local-file migration 0001: valid unbound files used by exactly one existing monitor bind automatically, counting paused monitors; shared and unused files remain unbound with explicit owner instructions. Scheduled checks record bounded non-secret binding diagnostics and never bind files. Missing or invalid references yield runner errors without falling back to unauthenticated requests. Raw secrets and raw response bodies never enter observations, alerts or archives; only EVIDENCE-002's redacted excerpt may be stored, separately, and travel in archives. Portable historical references are not receiving-installation execution authority.

Heartbeat tokens are owner-issued, hashed at rest, scoped to an immutable revision and rotated on issuance. Server receipt time and strictly increasing sequences prevent replay in the current header form; HEARTBEAT-002's URL-capability form is labeled replay-unprotected. Ingress alone cannot change state. A scheduled slot freezes an installation-local receipt snapshot; signed completion must match it. Missing, stale, future, paused, revision-mismatched or imported receipts cannot establish Healthy.

FLOW-004’s Chromium, Firefox and WebKit desktop/mobile execution and FLOW-003’s opt-in redacted failure artifacts are implemented. FLOW-001’s broader login/signup/checkout support qualification and FLOW-002’s reusable scripts retain their separate Status-table gaps. The following describes the constrained implementation and its retained safety obligations.

A flow is validated by the same function in the Worker, the definitions engine and the runner. Steps are `goto`, `click`, `fill` (a `credentialRef`, never a value), `waitFor` and `expect`; a target is exactly one of a plain CSS selector, text, label, or a role with its name. Required outcomes have an id and an expectation, and every one must be observed after the last step. Unknown step kinds and fields, scripts, other selector engines, secrets, intervals under 5 minutes, more than 20 steps or 8 outcomes, and more than 5 flows in an installation are refused with the entry named. Bounds per run: 60 seconds of wall time, 8 top-level pages, 5 MiB of response bytes, an 8 KiB trace; exceeding one fails the run and names it.

The runner serves a flow only through `runners/src/flow/`: its own process, a fresh 0700 profile deleted afterwards, an environment holding no inherited credential, proxy setting or Node hook, and the named credentials passed over a pipe. Chromium, Firefox and WebKit use the same authenticated filtering proxy inside the runner for pages, redirects, subresources and WebSockets. Engine-specific launch settings force proxy routing; page entry points for WebRTC and WebTransport are disabled before scripts run, service workers and downloads are blocked, and certificate verification remains enabled. The proxy resolves each destination itself and connects to the checked address. Public checks refuse private, loopback, link-local and metadata addresses; PRIVATE-001 grants authorize only their exact private targets, and the local fixture requires a synthetic grant. Each monitor fixes one browser and a desktop (1280 × 800) or mobile (390 × 844, touch, device scale 3) context. Firefox applies the mobile viewport/touch context without Playwright’s unsupported `isMobile` option. Signed evidence must match that immutable profile; independent network vantages evaluate the same profile, and reports and inactive archives retain it. A page may load top-level pages only on the origins the flow names and may not open a second window.

A flow runs a probe like any monitor, so incidents need the same vantage agreement. Failures keep distinct reasons (expected text or element missing, no element for a click, an error status, the wall limit, a forbidden address, a second origin, a missing outcome); a runner-side problem (no browser, a missing credential) is a runner error and the flow is Unknown. An observation's `flow.digest` must equal the digest of the flow in its slot's revision. Recovery compares the exact requirement set against the revision current when the open incident began: browser/device profile, required outcome ids with their expectations, and explicit `expect` steps. Removing or changing any original requirement, changing the browser/device profile, or switching monitor type makes a later pass a changed-definition recovery, labeled in state, recovery event and console with the revisions and removed requirements. Equal outcome counts cannot hide a changed expectation or profile; a pass in a new profile never proves the original profile recovered. Credentials are runner-local files bound to an exact origin and appear in no table, archive, export, log, trace or audit record. The flow tables are the existing monitor, revision, slot and observation tables; no table was added.

One import pipeline, Base's import door, serves the owner's Definitions view and local command (`/api/operator/import/*`, origin-bound, owner session, the source named per request) and Business grants (`/api/rer/import/*`), with one server-side source allow-list; the read-only definitions export and recognition (`/api/definitions/recognise`) write nothing, and a plan's preview reads the door's retained plan. Importers only split a source into entries and map each to a file entry or an unsupported/refused reason; planning, apply and undo are source-independent. Definition batches applied before the door keep their read and undo routes. The UptimeRobot adapter maps HTTP(S), keyword presence/absence and heartbeat monitors, preserving exact expected status codes, classes and ranges (defaulting to 2xx/3xx), supported methods, a timeout bounded to 50 ms–10 seconds and intervals from 5 seconds to one day. Its saved heartbeat `interval`/`gracePeriod` mapping and the saved Better Stack heartbeat-page `period`/`grace` mapping create paused definitions with newly issued local URL authority; these bounded import paths do not establish live source-account cutover. Site24x7’s heartbeat threshold conversion remains part of the missing MIGRATE-004 implementation. Heartbeats require a new owner-issued token and list the old URL for repointing. Keyword case differences, timeout changes and unsupported monitor types are named. Request authentication, headers and bodies become a local credential reference without source secrets. An initial-origin ignore-SSL setting is preserved as an explicit private-runner exception. Source regions, assigned contacts, status pages, maintenance, tags/groups and expiry reminders are listed rather than silently discarded. Imported monitors use local-a and need a second network or a canary before enabling.

Saved Pingdom HTTP check-detail responses also map cadence, URL, literal criteria, local credential references and explicit certificate verification through reviewed paused apply. Separately, the saved UptimeRobot webhook-create-payload door preserves supported JSON/form/query templates, variable aliases and header names, discards source secrets and names unavailable variables; opaque integration detail and unsupported delivery modes refuse explicitly. ROUTING-002 separately previews saved UptimeRobot per-contact threshold/recurrence and Pingdom delay/repeat/recovery settings against an explicit local destination map, through the same reviewed route apply door. These bounded saved-file paths do not establish live extraction, all-contact/history migration, sibling handoff or authorized source-account cutover under MIGRATE-001/MIGRATE-002.

A recognized log export reports its row count and provenance; no row becomes a slot, observation, state or incident, so imported history cannot satisfy quorum, recovery or availability figures. Storing that history as labeled source history for reports, without it ever becoming evidence, is HISTORY-001’s target. Migration 0026 adds `definition_batches` and `definition_batch_entries`; monitor erasure removes a monitor’s batch entries and operator erasure anonymizes batch actors. `tests/definitions-import.mjs`, `tests/tls-trust-journey.mjs` and `tests/webhook-custom.mjs` exercise these saved-file owner doors with synthetic source inputs; `tests/archive-roundtrip.mjs` exercises inactive archive behavior. No real source-account migration or hosted import is established.

A drill exists to check, one destination at a time, that an alert reaches somebody who can act. **Run alert drill** queues the test event with drill wording (`eventType` `uptime.notification.drill`, `kind` `test`, `incidentKey` null) for that destination's current credential. Disabled destinations can be drilled, as they can be tested. The one automatic attempt and the uncertain-never-resent rule are DELIVERY-001's. The message names who started the drill and when, and carries a link to `/alert-drill` holding a random 256-bit capability. Email has it as a text line and an HTML link, Slack as a message line, and the signed JSON webhook as an extra top-level `drill` object (`startedBy`, `startedAt`, `expiresAt`, `confirmUrl`) on drill events only. Incident events retain their immutable context; configurable webhook requests and payloads use WEBHOOK-001’s exact-byte signing. The default JSON envelope and Lamp-compatible signing remain available.

D1 stores the capability's SHA-256, bound to the drill, the destination and its credential. A copy sealed under the installation key lives only until the single send is over, and the runner reads it only while it holds that delivery's claim. The stored event, the stored webhook/Slack envelope, the archive and the console reads never contain the link. Opening the link (GET or HEAD) shows a page naming only the destination kind and the drill time. Only a same-origin form POST confirms, compared in constant time and accepted once within 24 hours. Unknown, used, expired and foreign links answer the ordinary 404 page, and the path is declared in `seed.json` under its own rate-limit class. The recipient needs no sign-in.
The console shows, per destination, "Last proven" (the latest confirmed drill for the current credential), "Not proven in 30 days" or "Never proven" in words, beside the latest drill's three lines:
**Submitted** is when Uptime started the one send. Before then it says the drill is queued, or why nothing was sent.
**Acknowledged** is when the provider or endpoint answered and with what code, or Uncertain or Failed with the code. Acknowledgment is not inbox receipt.
**Recipient confirmed** shows the time someone used the link, reported by the recipient. Until then it is pending, and after 24 hours it reads "not confirmed within 24 hours" with nothing sent again.

Whether anyone acted is not measured. The first-run page lists any destinations already present with the same proof words. Drill history (`alert_drills`) is installation-local: archives carry the drill's delivery history like any test send, but never the drill rows, so restored destinations start Never proven. Erasing a destination erases its drills; erasing an operator removes the operator reference from the drills they started. Unmeasured: no hosted drill to a real inbox or channel has been run (see ACCEPTANCE.md).

Versioned archives include definitions, immutable observations, state, product outbox events, notification history for source records that remain, erasure receipts, the permanent anonymized action audit, source identity and erasure journal, and an integrity digest. Legacy development sign-in records are installation-local, not archive data, and remain until their associated operator is erased or local reset; no captured-mail viewer or new sign-in capture is exposed. Restore validates bounded UTF8 bytes, schema, version, semantics and hash before transaction and requires empty product data. Existing receiving-owner, runner-registration and idle-contact records do not make product data nonempty and remain unchanged by restore. Imported monitors gain new paused current revisions; leases are interrupted and alerts quarantined. Derived attempt checkpoints, request credential values, heartbeat authority, sessions, keys, grants, contact, webhook and Slack URLs, and signing keys are installation-local and are not imported; destination definitions and retained notification histories are portable. A local CLI receiving checkout must first run `rer setup --owner-email EMAIL --non-interactive` to establish its owner and settings; setup leaves product data empty for import. No imported event or receipt automatically replays. A digest checks changed bytes, not trustworthy provenance. To restore a pre-erasure archive after an erasure, export the later source journal from Runner / Archive and provide it to restore; local CLI import accepts its absolute path in `UPTIME_LATER_JOURNAL`. By itself, an old offline archive cannot reveal later erasure when restored into a fresh installation that has never received that journal. This is a limit of Base's offline transfer model.

Observation metadata, monitor definitions, destination and delivery history, audit history, and legacy development sign-in records have no automatic age/count deletion. The maintenance sweep deletes expired operator sessions, old owner/auth rate-limit windows, expired public rate-limit rows and old login-attempt counters. Short-lived authorization rows can also expire logically without being deleted; expired discovery jobs are marked expired and retained. Drill expiry/confirmation clears only the one-time capability ciphertext/hash while retaining the drill row. Owner rotation/deletion retires endpoint credentials by scrubbing their secret material after active sends finish while keeping the credential/history row. The notification bridge removes an `integration_attempts` row only when it proves that the exact attempt never reached the send boundary; its delivery reservation and job remain. A setup migration removes stale, unclaimed dependency-approval state. Explicit owner erasure and local reset are separate destructive actions. Current migrations create 94 application tables. The RETENTION-001 runtime journey (`tests/retention-cleanup-proof.mjs`) inventories every migrated table and compares surviving identities across owner/runner cleanup, Cron and Worker restart. It covers expired native sessions and authentication/public counters, retained legacy records and expired authority, failure-snapshot content expiry, discovery status expiry, interrupted probe leases, drill capability scrubbing, in-flight credential rotation/retirement and proven-unsent attempt release; retained history and exact availability remain unchanged. View limits (100 history slots and 200 outbox entries), monitor limits and archive limits are not deletion rules. Deletion must never silently improve the configured denominator or historical health.

Monitor erasure removes its revisions, slots, observations, derived attempt checkpoints, heartbeat claims and authority, incident events, related notification jobs and deliveries, and archive-history copies. Destination erasure removes the destination, all credential versions, dependent notification jobs, delivery attempts and outcomes, replay entries and matching archive-history copies. Operator erasure removes that operator's sessions, tokens, invitations, legacy development sign-in credentials and messages. For the original owner, the bootstrap claim keeps its singleton and claim time but replaces the operator reference with an unrelated anonymous UUID. Its receipt counts that row as anonymized, and the source journal fences its original primary key. The replacement commits in the same guarded batch as account deletion; setup remains claimed and receiving-installation authority remains local. The audit remains separate from the erased entity: its subject reference is opaque, and actor references for an erased operator become anonymized. Erasure writes a durable receipt with per-table counts and completion time in the same D1 batch as its audit record, deletion and Base portability erasure-fence statements.

The audit includes destructive actions and automated notification attempts, including test sends, plus operator authentication-mail provider attempts and legacy development capture history. The mail sender records the feature audit before attempting the provider request. Actor and subject fields are identifiers or feature names, never user-supplied names, emails, URLs or secrets. The audit travels in product archives. A later erasure journal makes restore refuse old audit actor references for an erased operator. Older offline archive bytes and external messages already sent cannot be changed by a later local erasure; a request already in progress may still reach its provider. Uptime does not use R2 for attachments; it does accept import-door uploads in D1. On operator or destination erasure, all import-door uploads (including interrupted uploads), snapshot and kit content and undo custody are withdrawn, approval identities and archive labels are anonymized, and only approval times/fingerprints, opaque lineage and archive receipt metadata remain, with native monitors preserved. This conservative rule applies with Business disabled because indivisible exports have no reliable operator/destination membership index. Approval rows keep their plan links, but caller-supplied approval/reviewer ids are replaced; archive headers keep hashes, sizes, counts and times while their filename/tool labels and caller-supplied upload references are replaced. Public import history labels retired jobs as history only and offers no undo; old snapshot operations and archive restore-check refuse withdrawn content. Installation opt-in, grant replay metadata and permanent key revocations remain. Monitor-level custody erasure retains its existing monitor-specific scope.

Authenticated runner contact records control-plane receipt time for accepted scoped claims, including idle claims, and accepted signed results. Owner reads, health checks and rejected requests do not refresh it. Fresh means within 120 seconds; future or unverifiable time is stale. Contact does not prove process liveness or target success. Restart retains it, archives omit it, and failed overview reads label contact unavailable with any prior timestamp clearly historical.

The interface exposes textual state, freshness, reasons, immutable revisions and manual provenance, with labels, keyboard controls and responsive layout. Failed reads show Unknown and last successful refresh. Action errors persist across polling; busy controls stay excluded through reconciliation. Editing must preserve configured checks; duplicated reserved typed assertion keys are rejected rather than silently overriding criteria. Route forms, reviewed previews and saved summaries show each contact’s delay, repeat interval and cap, recovery preference and stop-on-acknowledgment policy. The saved UptimeRobot/Pingdom schedule preview requires an explicit source-contact-to-local-destination map and makes no writes until reviewed apply. Incident reads expose the next due contact follow-up. No fabricated uptime figure or color-only state is acceptable.

Email, signed webhook and Slack destinations are installation-local definitions. Confirmed incident triggers select recipients from the first non-inherited policy in monitor → service → group → installation order, using the monitor’s current service and group labels in the event transaction. Installation defaults to all enabled destinations or an explicit selection; narrower scopes inherit or select their own list, and an empty selection explicitly means no recipients. Previews show selected and excluded recipients, disabled or missing destinations, unavailable credentials or mail configuration, and affected monitors including narrower overrides. Apply requires the reviewed digest and current revisions, refuses stale inputs and records durable route-change history and audit. ROUTING-002 snapshots each selected contact’s policy at confirmation: a 0–24-hour delay, repeats off or every 1 minute–24 hours with an optional cap, recovery preference and whether acknowledgment stops repeats. Delayed triggers require the same open incident; recovery inside the delay suppresses both that trigger and its recovery notice. Repeats are distinct durable reminder events with the original incident identity, stop on recovery or the selected acknowledgment policy, and survive restart without a burst of missed reminders. Acknowledgment preserves a still-open incident’s delayed initial notice while stopping repeats when selected. Recovery keeps the original trigger’s destination and credential, honors its recovery preference and waits for that trigger to be accepted; rejected or uncertain triggers cannot authorize recovery, and newly selected contacts receive no recovery for an incident they missed. Disabled, erased or rotated contacts do not silently count as covered. Saved UptimeRobot threshold and recurrence settings and Pingdom result-count delay/repeat/recovery settings preview onto explicitly mapped local contacts; Pingdom counts are multiplied by its check resolution in minutes. Historically, teams, environment/severity/region/origin and business-hour and quiet-hour rules, portable route settings and history and expiry and renewal routing were ROUTING-001 gaps. Current accepted rows record the implemented team, environment/severity/origin filters and contact quiet holds; business hours, basic geographic routing and UI acceptance, portable route settings and history and expiry and renewal remain open. Unlanded routing branch evidence is not accepted-main provenance. Expiry and renewal notices still use installation-wide destinations. Route settings and detailed route history stay local; archives retain opaque audit entries. The hosted Worker submits email through the configured Base mail adapter and sends webhooks and Slack without a private runner; a private runner can also claim notification work. The one-time test action queues a distinct test event and does not change monitor state. Only scheduled incident transitions create outage trigger and recovery notifications; maintenance suppresses these events, and manual checks do not create them. ROUTING-002 creates correlated reminders from the saved contact schedule; SLOW-001 independently creates Slow, slow-reminder and slow-recovered events without changing availability or opening outage incidents. Portable archives include destination kind, name, enabled setting and available email address, but exclude webhook and Slack URLs, signing keys and other credentials; delivery envelopes travel without the request body they sent, which restore rebuilds from the archived event. Restored destinations are disabled until the receiving owner reauthorizes and enables them.

In the current implementation signed-webhook incident deliveries retry with a stable key and stored backoff times; email, Slack, unsigned webhooks, tests and drills keep one automatic send attempt; ROUTING-002 reminders are new correlated events, not retries of an earlier uncertain send. A selected route can name up to three ordered fallback contacts and an uncertain deadline, snapshotted with each confirmed trigger or DEPENDENCY-002 dependency notice; only incident triggers and dependency notices escalate, and reminders, slow notices, tests and drills never do. Email and fallback attempts are recorded like webhook attempts, without bodies or credentials. A RER relay 429 with Retry-After queues an unaccepted message until that delay expires. For destinations without receiver deduplication, HTTP 500, timeouts, connection loss, and unclassified responses remain uncertain without automatic resend. A successful provider or endpoint response means only that the request was acknowledged. It is not proof of inbox delivery, a person reading it, or an operational response. Authentication mail remains separate from incident email. A single runner is one network vantage; logical probe names do not establish geographic independence. WEBHOOK-001 now supplies configurable methods, content types, encrypted custom headers and JSON/form/query templates with UptimeRobot aliases, exact-byte signing, previews and bounded redacted receiver outcomes. NOTICE-001’s email, Slack and webhook notices retain the original failure, failed locations, incident link, captured owner IANA zone/UTC offset and exact confirmed downtime across restart and inactive restore. New incidents capture the selected zone; existing incidents keep theirs. CHAT-001, PHONE-001, PHONE-002, MOBILE-001’s native clients/push, ONCALL-001, LAMP-001 and INCIDENT-001’s mention email remain beyond the implemented channels. Full responder rotations and public communication remain owned by the named sibling products. The cited local three-engine execution evidence does not establish production network placement, recipient acceptance or full accessibility conformance; those require separate validation.

Judgement clarification (23 October 2026): the preceding implementation narrative describes the earlier channel boundary. INCIDENT-001 now has bounded explicit-member mention email through Base, with fresh ACCESS-001 scopes and single-attempt custody proven in `tests/incident-work.mjs`; held console workflows remain a Gap. Its Status row gives the current partial verdict and the original acceptance clause remains unchanged.
Notification endpoints and webhook signing keys are authenticated encrypted
at rest under installation-local Worker-secret custody. Rotation cancels
queued work using the old credential. Once no send is in progress, retirement
scrubs endpoint, signing key and ciphertext and sets `retired_at`; the credential
row identity and committed delivery history remain. A genuinely sending obsolete
version retains its material only until its outcome. Destination erasure removes
all credential versions and dependent local delivery history. Slack uses its
capability URL alone and has no Uptime signing key.
The key-bearing upgrade encrypts retained credentials, cancels obsolete queued
work and scrubs unused or terminal versions. A genuinely sending obsolete
version remains available only until its outcome. Individual undecryptable
credentials fail closed without disabling monitoring or sign-in; the owner can
re-enter or delete them. Email addresses are readable by the authenticated
owner; URL credentials and signing keys never appear in destination lists.
Destination comparison hashes use purpose-derived HMAC custody. An ahead
runner leaves queued work available to a correctly timed runner. Only an owned,
fresh and durably unstarted claim can return to the queue; its reservation
identity is retained separately from network attempts. Started, expired and
uncertain attempts are never automatically replayed.
Durable route-visible outcomes have been measured for exhausted HTTP, keyword
and heartbeat retries, abandoned leases, discovery outcomes, notification
failures/uncertainty and drill expiry. The flow retention run canceled before

browser launch; it does not establish browser-execution acceptance. OPS-001 now retains Worker watch, external-heartbeat and authentication-mail attempts and outcomes in `auxiliary_attempts`, with expired leases reconciled after restart. The private runner keeps outage/recovery progress and attempt history in its protected local SQLite journal across SIGKILL, including interruption at unreachable and recovery send boundaries. A submitted attempt with no confirmed outcome becomes Uncertain and never replays; unsubmitted expired work remains distinct. Auxiliary history restores inactive at ARCHIVE-001 bounds without dispatch authority. These durable paths replace the former BASE-OPS-004 latest-only/in-memory gap; independent hosted placement and human recipient acceptance remain separate requirements.

TCP, DNS, TLS and domain settings survive archive export/restore/re-export with their exact immutable historical revisions and slot definitions. Current definitions restore paused with Unknown state and interrupted slots; repeated restore preserves the sanitized originals. Non-secret HTTP/browser credential references and monitor IDs survive archive restore; credential files and local runner authority never travel. A definitions import creates fresh IDs and receives no authority over existing files.

The complete product archive includes notification destination kind, name, enabled setting and available email address, incident/outbox events, notification jobs, delivery envelopes, attempts, resolutions and received replay history for records still in the source. Email addresses are definitions decrypted only through the installation secret-bound custody implementation; unavailable active email definitions cause explicit export refusal. Legacy soft-deleted destination rows that remain in a source database may appear with their remaining definition fields. Current destination erasure removes the row and its dependent notification history before later exports; its receipt and audit remain. Webhook and Slack URLs, signing keys, credential versions, claims, sessions, runner/heartbeat authority, synthetic grants and request credential values are excluded. Schema 2 has an explicit versioned product-table extension; prior six-table schema 2 and legacy schema 1 remain accepted.

Restore preserves sanitized original state and notification history in a flat content-addressed archive-history ledger while live definitions are paused/disabled, queued or running slots interrupted, outbox quarantined and jobs prevented from dispatch. No imported event is replayed. Exports refuse named 10,000-row per-table, 100-monitor and 2 MiB bounds rather than truncate; ARCHIVE-002 sets the target scale. Local `rer export --output FILE` and `rer import --input FILE --yes` use the same archive implementation as the console with private regular archive files and installation settings. Before local import, setup must establish the receiving owner and private settings; product and history tables must remain empty. Empty-product validation covers product/history tables, including orphan histories, while preserving owner identity, migration history and exact private settings. The explicit schema inventory classifies authentication identities, authorization audits, development sign-in mail and dispatch reservations as installation-local authority. Unknown tables or foreign integration namespaces cause named export refusal rather than omission. The replacement proof is `tests/archive-roundtrip.mjs`, which checks complete portable records and byte-preserved originals against each explicit inactive-restore transformation.

The BASE-DATA-001 installation-authority and endpoint-credential exclusion is the owner-accepted policy dated 2026-10-13; available email addresses remain portable destination definitions. This is the recorded replacement for this edition, not full BASE-DATA-001 equivalence.

Uptime uses Base's portable rer CLI with Node 22.20.0 and pnpm 10.12.4. Setup establishes the first owner, uses configured email-link sign-in and local dev identity, preserves prior owner/data/settings and stops its temporary app. Dev provides real Vite assets/HMR. The canonical local state is `.wrangler/state`; unexpected state placement requires explicit recovery. Reset is confirmed and contained; builds exclude and restore private settings. CLI archives use Base integrity and named payloads around the complete Uptime archive, including the audit and source erasure journal, and atomic inactive restore. The console archive format and historical restore policy remain supported. Remote CLI transfer is unavailable. Deployment and hosted acceptance remain separate.
Signed Assisted admission uses `/auth/owner-claim`, trusted installation bindings
and hidden setup credentials, followed by the same native owner session. A
second valid signature cannot replace a claimed owner. Native bootstrap remains supported.
`/api/editor/config` is an owner-only private no-store route; the editor receives
no setup, session or provider secrets. See `scripts/delivery/README.md`.

See [resilient monitoring](docs/resilient-monitoring.md) for runner-local unreachable/recovery notices, Worker stale-contact email, optional external heartbeat pings and weekly all-healthy digest.
